opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the things they deserve real credit for is that they've tried to make their forecasts concrete enough to be wrong. A lot of discussion about transformative AI happens at a level of vagueness where almost any future could be read as confirming your view. Phrases like "AGI soon" or "things will get really weird" don't commit you to much. What I appreciate about their scenario work is that they lay out a sequence of developments, with rough timings and intermediate milestones, so that as the next couple of years unfold you can actually check: are we on this path or not?

That said, I have some reservations about how it's interpreted. When you write a single detailed scenario, there's a natural tendency for readers to treat it as *the* prediction, the modal outcome. But a story with many specific steps is necessarily less probable than any one of its components. Each additional detail makes it more vivid and more persuasive, and at the same time less likely. That's the classic conjunction problem. I think the authors understand this, and they've been fairly clear that it's one illustrative path and that their actual timelines have wide uncertainty. But the format itself pulls attention toward the specific story rather than the distribution.

So what I'd like to see, and to some degree they've done this, is a clearer separation between three things. First, the underlying probability distributions over key quantities, such as when we get systems that can substantially automate AI research. Second, the scenario, which is one coherent sample from that space, chosen to be roughly central. And third, the specific signposts that would cause them to update. That last part is the most useful for the rest of us. If they say "by such-and-such date we'd expect to see agents reliably doing tasks of this length," and that doesn't happen, we should be able to see clearly how much that pushes their whole picture back.

There's also a subtler issue about what counts as the prediction coming true. If the milestones arrive a year or two late, is that a vindication or a miss? In one sense it's a remarkable success, because most people would have been off by decades. In another sense, the policy recommendations often depend quite sensitively on timing. I think it's worth being explicit up front about which aspects of the forecast matter most and how much slippage would change the bottom line.

So overall, I'm positive about it. It's the kind of thing I'd like more people in this space to do. But I'd encourage readers to hold the narrative lightly and focus on the measurable claims, and I'd encourage the authors to keep foregrounding those claims, so that the scenario becomes a tool for learning rather than a story people either buy into or reject wholesale.

r001.rationale: The response praises concrete scenarios and recommends distinguishing distributions, scenarios, and signposts, but it does not endorse providing separate forecasts for multiple formulations of the forecast question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the AI Futures Project deserves a lot of credit for the way they went about it, actually. The thing that frustrates me about most AI forecasting is that it's so vague you can never tell afterwards whether the person was right. Someone says "transformative AI by 2030" and then in 2030 there's an argument about what "transformative" meant, and everyone retreats to the version of the claim that looks best in hindsight. That's not really forecasting at all, in the sense that matters. It's more like prophecy, where the ambiguity is doing most of the work.

What they tried to do with AI 2027 was to write down a concrete scenario — month by month, with specific capabilities, specific compute figures, specific things that happen in labs and in government — and then say, in effect, "this is roughly what we expect, and here is the reasoning behind each step." You can disagree with it, and I do disagree with parts of it, but you can disagree with it precisely. You can point at the step where you think the timeline breaks and explain why. And when reality diverges, as it already has in some respects, you can see where and by how much. That's enormously valuable, because it turns a debate about vibes into a debate about mechanisms.

Where I'd push back a little is that a single detailed scenario carries a kind of rhetorical weight that's out of proportion to its probability. Any specific story about the future, told in enough detail, is almost certainly false in its particulars. They know this — they're quite explicit that the mode of their distribution and the median are different things, and that the scenario is one draw rather than the expected outcome. But readers don't absorb that caveat very well. People remember the narrative, not the error bars. So there's a tension between wanting to be concrete enough to be falsifiable and not wanting to give false precision about something that's genuinely very uncertain.

The other thing I'd say is that I think the most important predictions aren't really the dates. Whether superhuman coding arrives in 2027 or 2031 matters less than the structural claims: that AI research itself becomes the bottleneck that gets automated, that this produces a feedback loop, that the geopolitical dynamics push labs and governments toward racing rather than caution. Those are the claims that should get the scrutiny, and they're harder to specify in a way that can be cleanly checked. I'd like to see more effort go into making those parts as crisp as the capability milestones.

But on the whole, I think it's a model for how this ought to be done. If you're going to make claims about the future that you want people to act on, you owe them something they can hold you to. They did that, and I wish more people would.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises the project for specifying a concrete scenario and making its claims checkable, but does not endorse providing separate forecasts for multiple formulations of the forecast question.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the strengths of their approach is that they try to make the forecasts concrete enough that you can tell what would count as being wrong. With AI, people often make predictions using terms like “AGI” or “superintelligence”, but those can conceal quite different expectations. Two people might appear to disagree about timelines when they’re actually predicting different things.

Specifying the capabilities you expect, and what would demonstrate those capabilities, helps enormously. It lets other people scrutinise the prediction, and it gives you a better chance of learning from how things turn out.

The qualification I’d make is that precision isn’t the same as accuracy. A very detailed scenario can be useful for making assumptions explicit, but we shouldn’t interpret all that detail as something the forecaster can reliably foresee. I’d want to distinguish the central claims they’re forecasting from the illustrative details used to tell the story.

r001.rationale: The response supports making forecasts concrete and clarifying what capabilities they predict, but it does not endorse providing separate forecasts for multiple formulations of the question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot to be said for trying to specify exactly what you’re predicting. With AI, people can appear to disagree quite sharply and then discover that they meant different things by “human-level” or “transformative.” Making the claim concrete helps us see whether there’s a substantive disagreement, and it gives us a chance to learn when the forecast turns out to be wrong.

The thing I’d be careful about is distinguishing a detailed scenario from a prediction that all those details will happen. You might think a scenario illustrates a very plausible way things could unfold while assigning quite a low probability to that exact sequence. So I’d want clarity both about the events being forecast and about which parts are illustrative. Precision about what a claim means is very valuable; it shouldn’t be confused with certainty that the claim is true.

r001.rationale: The response endorses making predictions concrete and clarifying what they mean, but it does not endorse providing separate forecasts for multiple formulations of the question.
